title: What All Universal Data Means
body:
All universal data is universe-scale reference data: the catalogs, constants, frames, and standards that describe the universe as a whole, from the constants of physics to the positions of stars, galaxies, and spacecraft.

Where all world's data inventories Earth's public data, all universal data inventories the reference data astronomers, physicists, and space agencies use to locate objects, measure time, and compare observations made years apart and continents apart.

This database keeps a firm line between measured fact, derived standard, and inference. Constants with exact SI definitions are stated as exact. Measured quantities carry their uncertainty. Dark matter and dark energy are labeled as inferred, because their presence is deduced from gravitational and expansion effects rather than direct observation.

The records that follow move from the overview through catalogs, constants, missions, structure, frames, and time standards, and they close with cross-links back to all world's data, so Earth-scale and universe-scale inventories form one navigable system.

print("units and frame stated in body")

title: Astronomy Catalogs: The Reference Lists of the Sky
body:
Astronomy catalogs are the reference lists of the sky: systematic compilations of stars, galaxies, nebulae, and other objects, each entry carrying a position, a brightness, and an identifier that other observers can reuse.

A catalog is useful only when its entries are stable. An object keeps its identifier across decades, its position is given in a stated reference frame, and later catalogs can be matched against earlier ones so the same object is never counted twice under two names.

Modern catalogs are built from surveys that scan large areas of sky repeatedly. Repeated observation separates real, persistent objects from artifacts, measures how objects move or vary over time, and lets catalogs grow by adding fainter objects without rewriting earlier entries.

To use an astronomy catalog, state the catalog, the reference frame, and the epoch of its positions. Those three facts are what make a position in one catalog comparable with a position in another.

title: Physics Constants: The Fixed Numbers of Nature
body:
Physics constants are the fixed numbers that appear across physics. Some are now exact by definition in the International System of Units, and some remain measured quantities whose values improve as experiments improve.

The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second by SI definition, and it defines the metre itself. The Planck constant is exactly 6.62607015 times ten to the power of minus 34 joule-seconds, and the elementary charge is exactly 1.602176634 times ten to the power of minus 19 coulombs.

The Newtonian gravitational constant is a measured quantity, approximately 6.67430 times ten to the power of minus 11 cubic metres per kilogram per second squared, with a small experimental uncertainty. It is never quoted here without that qualification, because quoting a measured constant as exact would misstate the science.

Constants are the bridge between universal data and everyday measurement: they let a laboratory result, a spacecraft trajectory, and a stellar observation all be expressed in the same units and checked against one another.

title: Space Missions: Real Missions by Name and Year
body:
Space missions are recorded here by name and year only, without invented detail. Sputnik 1 launched in 1957 as the first artificial satellite. Apollo 11 landed people on the Moon in 1969. Voyager 1 launched in 1977 and continues outward through interplanetary space.

Later missions extended the same story: the Hubble Space Telescope launched in 1990, Cassini launched in 1997 toward Saturn, and the James Webb Space Telescope launched in 2021. Each name and year is a matter of public record, and this database adds no mission detail beyond what public sources establish.

A mission record earns its place by what it returned: observations, measurements, or samples that entered the public catalogs and standards. Missions are therefore cross-linked to the catalogs and constants they improved, rather than listed as isolated achievements.

Readers who need mission detail should consult the mission's own public archive. This inventory's job is to place each mission in the universe-scale reference system and to keep its name and year exact.

title: Cosmic Structure: Galaxies, Clusters, Filaments, and Voids
body:
Cosmic structure is the large-scale arrangement of matter in the universe. Galaxies gather into groups and clusters, clusters link along filaments of galaxies and gas, and between the filaments lie vast voids where galaxies are sparse.

This structure grew from tiny density differences in the early universe, amplified by gravity over billions of years. The filament-and-void pattern, sometimes called the cosmic web, is the largest pattern known, spanning hundreds of millions of light-years.

Catalogs of galaxies are what make the cosmic web visible. A galaxy's position and distance turn a list of points into a three-dimensional map, and maps from many surveys together reveal filaments, clusters, and voids as real structures rather than chance groupings.

To describe a structure honestly, give its scale, the survey it was mapped from, and the uncertainty in its distances. A filament claimed without a survey and a distance scale is a picture, not a measurement.

title: Universal Reference Frames: ICRS and Galactic Coordinates
body:
A reference frame is the coordinate system against which positions are stated. Without a stated frame, a position is a pair of numbers with no meaning, because different frames place the same object at different coordinates.

The International Celestial Reference System, ICRS, is the standard celestial frame, defined by the positions of distant extragalactic radio sources that show no measurable proper motion. It replaced earlier frames tied to Earth's moving equator and equinox, and it is stable at a level far finer than most observations require.

Galactic coordinates are a second frame, centered on the Sun, with latitude measured from the plane of the Milky Way and longitude measured from the direction of the galactic center. They are the natural frame for describing where objects sit within our own galaxy.

Every catalog record in this database states its frame. Converting between frames is a defined mathematical operation, and the reference-frames guide record in this database explains those conversions in usable form.

title: Time Standards: UTC, TAI, and TT
body:
Time standards let observations made years apart be compared on one clock. Three standards matter most: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), International Atomic Time (TAI), and Terrestrial Time (TT).

TAI is built from atomic clocks around the world and runs uniformly, without leap seconds. UTC is the civil time standard, kept close to Earth's rotation by the occasional insertion of leap seconds, so UTC and TAI differ by a whole number of seconds that grows over time.

Terrestrial Time is the theoretical time scale for ephemerides and Earth-surface observations, defined so that TT minus TAI is exactly 32.184 seconds. That exact offset is what lets a TT time be converted to TAI without ambiguity.

To use a time standard correctly, state which one a timestamp belongs to. A UTC timestamp, a TAI timestamp, and a TT timestamp for the same event differ, and mixing them silently introduces errors larger than many measurements can tolerate.

title: Stellar Catalogs: Positions, Brightness, and Motion
body:
Stellar catalogs record stars the way astronomy catalogs record all sky objects, with the added detail that stars move. A stellar entry therefore carries position, brightness, and, where measured, proper motion and parallax distance.

Parallax is the geometric foundation of stellar distances: as Earth orbits the Sun, a nearby star appears to shift against distant background stars, and the size of that shift gives its distance directly. Catalogs built on parallax measurements anchor the whole cosmic distance ladder.

Proper motion extends a catalog through time. A star's position at a stated epoch, plus its proper motion, lets its position be predicted for other epochs, so catalogs from different decades remain comparable.

The honest use of a stellar catalog states its epoch, its frame, and its limiting brightness. A catalog complete to one brightness is not a census of all stars, only of all stars brighter than its limit.

title: Exoplanets: Worlds Around Other Stars
body:
Exoplanets are planets orbiting stars other than the Sun. Thousands are confirmed, found chiefly by the transit method, in which a planet dims its star as it passes in front of it, and by the radial-velocity method, in which a planet's gravity makes its star wobble.

Each confirmed exoplanet carries an orbital period, a size or mass estimate, and a host star. Those three facts, with their uncertainties, are what separate a confirmed planet from a candidate signal that still needs confirmation.

Exoplanet catalogs grow by confirmation, not by announcement. A candidate enters the catalog as confirmed only when independent evidence rules out false positives such as eclipsing binary stars or stellar activity mimicking a planet.

The scientific value of the exoplanet catalog is statistical as much as individual: the distribution of planet sizes, orbits, and host stars is what reveals how planetary systems form and how common Earth-sized worlds may be.

title: Cosmology: Expansion and the Hubble Constant
body:
Cosmology is the study of the universe as a whole: its expansion, its age, its composition, and its future. Its central observation is that distant galaxies recede from us, with recession speed broadly proportional to distance.

The Hubble constant expresses that proportionality, in units of kilometres per second per megaparsec. Its value is measured, not defined, and different measurement methods have given values roughly in the range from 67 to 73 kilometres per second per megaparsec.

That range is stated here deliberately, with its uncertainty, and never collapsed to a single false-precise value. The disagreement between early-universe and late-universe measurements is a live research question, and an honest database reports the tension rather than hiding it behind one number.

Cosmology's other quantities, the age of the universe and its composition, inherit the same discipline: values with uncertainties, methods stated, and revisions recorded when better measurements arrive.

title: Planetary Data: The Worlds of the Solar System
body:
Planetary data records the planets, dwarf planets, and moons of the Solar System: their orbits, sizes, masses, compositions, and surfaces, as measured by telescopes and spacecraft.

Orbital data is the most exact part of planetary science. A planet's orbital period and distance from the Sun are known to high precision, and they follow the same gravitational laws that govern spacecraft trajectories, so planetary data and mission navigation check one another.

Surface and atmosphere data is messier and more revisable. A planet's weather, surface age, or atmospheric composition changes as new spacecraft observations arrive, and this database treats those entries as current best measurements with stated sources, not as permanent facts.

To use planetary data well, separate orbital facts, which are stable, from surface and atmosphere facts, which are revised. Both belong in the record, labeled by how firmly each is known.

title: Asteroid and Comet Records: Small Bodies, Real Consequences
body:
Asteroids and comets are the Solar System's small bodies. Asteroids are mostly rocky or metallic and orbit chiefly between Mars and Jupiter and elsewhere in the system; comets are icy bodies that develop glowing comas and tails when they approach the Sun.

Small-body records carry an orbit, a size estimate, and an observation history. Orbits are refined every time a body is re-observed, so a small-body record is a living entry whose precision improves with each apparition.

Some near-Earth asteroids are tracked specifically because their orbits bring them close to Earth. Tracking them is a public safety function as well as a scientific one: a well-determined orbit is what turns a worrying first observation into a reliable long-term forecast.

Comet records add activity to the same framework: how bright the comet became, how its tail developed, and when it will return. Both kinds of record share the discipline of stated orbits, stated uncertainties, and open observation histories.

title: Dark Matter and Dark Energy: Inferred, Not Directly Observed
body:
Dark matter and dark energy are labeled in this database as inferred, not directly observed. That label is not a dismissal; it is the precise statement of their evidential status, and it is kept on every record that mentions them.

Dark matter is inferred from gravitational effects that visible matter cannot explain: galaxies rotate faster than their visible mass allows, and clusters bend light more than their visible matter predicts. Some form of additional gravitating matter, or a modification of gravity, is required by those observations.

Dark energy is inferred from the accelerating expansion of the universe, measured from distant supernovae and other cosmological probes. It is the name for whatever drives that acceleration, and its nature remains one of the largest open questions in physics.

An honest universal database keeps inference labeled as inference. Readers can then follow the evidence, weigh alternatives, and see exactly where measurement ends and interpretation begins.

title: Universal Constants Table: Values and Units Together
body:
A constants table is useful only when every value travels with its unit. A bare number without a unit is not a constant; it is a puzzle, and this table refuses to present one.

The table's exact entries, by SI definition, are: speed of light in vacuum, 299,792,458 metres per second; Planck constant, 6.62607015 times ten to the power of minus 34 joule-seconds; elementary charge, 1.602176634 times ten to the power of minus 19 coulombs.

Its measured entries carry uncertainties: the gravitational constant, approximately 6.67430 times ten to the power of minus 11 cubic metres per kilogram per second squared, with experimental uncertainty in its final digits; the Hubble constant, roughly 67 to 73 kilometres per second per megaparsec, method-dependent.

The table also records the exact TT minus TAI offset of 32.184 seconds, because time standards are constants of practice as much as constants of nature, and a universal database that omits them leaves its timestamps uninterpretable.

title: Reference-Frames Guide: Converting Between Frames
body:
This guide turns the reference-frames record into usable practice: how to state a frame, how to convert between frames, and how to avoid the errors that come from mixing them.

The first rule is declaration. Every position, catalog entry, and observation in this database names its frame, ICRS, galactic, or another stated system, and its epoch where motion matters. An undeclared frame is treated as an incomplete record.

The second rule is conversion by defined rotation. ICRS to galactic coordinates is a fixed rotation of the coordinate axes, published as a standard transformation. It is mathematics, not estimation, and two correct implementations agree to the precision of their arithmetic.

The third rule is epoch care. A stellar position at one epoch is not the same numbers at another epoch when proper motion is significant. Convert the epoch with the star's motion, or state that the position is epoch-specific and must not be compared directly with other epochs.

title: Measurement Units: SI and Astronomical Units
body:
Measurement units are the shared language of universal data. The International System of Units provides the base: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela, with derived units such as the joule and the coulomb built from them.

Astronomy adds its own working units, and this record defines them plainly. The astronomical unit is the mean Earth-Sun distance, about 149.6 million kilometres. The light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometres. The parsec, about 3.26 light-years, is the distance at which one astronomical unit subtends one arcsecond.

Unit discipline is what keeps universal data comparable. A distance in parsecs, a speed in kilometres per second, and a time in a stated standard can be combined; the same quantities in unstated or mixed units cannot, and this database rejects unstated units as incomplete data.

Every record in this database therefore states its units alongside its values, and the constants table record is the single place where the most-used values and units are gathered for quick checking.

title: Cross-Links: Universal Data Meets All World's Data
body:
Universal data and all world's data are companion inventories, not rivals. All world's data organizes Earth's public data by subject domain; all universal data organizes universe-scale reference data by catalog, constant, frame, and standard.

The cross-links run in both directions. Earth-observation source families in all world's data, such as NASA Earthdata, NOAA, and USGS, feed directly into universal catalogs and frames, because Earth-observing satellites and ground stations are also astronomical and geodetic instruments.

Conversely, universal standards return to Earth: time standards govern civil time and navigation, reference frames govern mapping and surveying, and constants govern every laboratory measurement that enters a world's-data domain record.

A reader who follows a cross-link from either inventory to the other should find the same discipline: stated frames, stated units, stated uncertainties, and labeled inference. That shared discipline is what makes two inventories one system.

title: The Cosmic Microwave Background: The Oldest Light
body:
The cosmic microwave background is the oldest light observable: radiation released when the early universe cooled enough for atoms to form, about 380,000 years after the beginning, and stretched by expansion into microwaves.

Its temperature is nearly uniform across the sky, about 2.725 kelvin, with tiny variations of roughly one part in a hundred thousand. Those variations are the seeds of cosmic structure, the same density differences that gravity later amplified into galaxies, filaments, and voids.

The background's spectrum matches a blackbody with extraordinary precision, which is why it counts as strong evidence for a hot, dense early universe. A spectrum that did not match would have falsified the picture; the match is what makes the background a cornerstone rather than a curiosity.

Background maps are catalogs in their own right: full-sky maps whose hot and cold spots encode the universe's age, composition, and geometry, and whose analysis continues to refine every cosmological quantity in this database.

title: Gravitational-Wave Catalogs: Ripples in Spacetime
body:
Gravitational-wave catalogs record ripples in spacetime produced by accelerating massive bodies, most strongly by merging black holes and neutron stars. Detectors measure the stretching and squeezing of space itself as a wave passes.

Each catalog entry carries the masses of the merging bodies, their distance, and the time of the event, all with uncertainties. The first direct detection, in 2015, opened a new observational window: astronomy by gravitational waves alongside astronomy by light.

Gravitational-wave astronomy complements light-based catalogs because it sees what light cannot: merging black holes emit no light to observe, yet their waves carry precise information about their masses and spins.

The catalog grows event by event, and each event is confirmed only after detector artifacts and noise are ruled out. That confirmation discipline is what keeps a catalog of invisible events trustworthy.

title: Stewardship: Provenance, Versioning, and Revision
body:
Stewardship is the discipline that keeps universal data usable across decades. A catalog entry without provenance, without a version, and without a revision history is a claim that cannot be checked, and this database does not accept one.

Provenance states the survey, instrument, and publication behind each entry. Versioning states which release of a catalog an entry came from, because catalogs are revised and an entry's value can change between releases. Revision history states what changed and why.

The same discipline applies to constants and standards. An exact SI constant never changes by measurement, but a measured constant's value and uncertainty do improve, and the database records each improvement as a new version rather than silently overwriting the old value.

Stewardship closes the universal inventory as it closes the world's inventory: every fact traceable, every revision visible, and every inference labeled, so that a reader a century from now can still check what was known, when it was known, and how firmly.
